pages.text: Once you advance far enough in your world, you may want to measure certain conditions, such as the wind speed or the time of the day.
The first is the $(thing)Precision Clock$(). The Clock detects the hour, or, when toggled with $(item)$(k:key.use)$(), the month.

When in hour mode, the clock will output a strong analog signal where signal 0 means midnight or noon, and signal 11 means 11:00 or 23:00.$(br2)When in month mode, the clock will output a strong analog signal where signal 0 means January, and signal 11 means December.$(br2)You do not need a comparator to read the Clock's signal strength.
Next we have the $(thing)Thermometer$(), which detects the ambient temperature, or the temperature of the device it is placed onto.

When reading ambient temperature, the Thermometer will output a strong analog signal where signal 0 means -40°C, and signal 15 means 40°C.$(br2)When reading device temperature, the Thermometer will output a weak analog signal where signal 0 means no heat, and signal 15 means Brilliant White.$(br2)You do not need a comparator to read the Thermometer's signal strength.

$(item)Mercury$() can be extracted from $(item)Cinnabar$().$(br2)If you're having trouble getting the Mercury into a vial, try using a $(l:craftsmanship/pottery#vessel)Vessel$() to transfer it into a $(l:craftsmanship/barrels)Barrel$(), and then $(item)$(k:key.use)$() the Vial on the barrel.
The glass vial is also able to carry around variable amounts of fluids like a $(item)Wooden Bucket$(), and can safely hold $(thing)Acids$().

The $(thing)Anemometer$() detects the wind speed. It outputs a strong analog signal where signal 0 means 0kmh, and signal 15 means 115 kmh.$(br2)You do not need a comparator to read the Anemometer's signal strength.

The $(thing)Weather Vane$() detects the wind direction. It outputs a strong analog signal where signal 0 means North, and signal 8 means south. The signal increases as the wind direction proceeds clockwise.$(br2)You do not need a comparator to read the Weather Vane's signal strength.

pages.title: More Redstone
pages.text: Want to do more with redstone? Check out what the $(item)More Red$() mod has to offer, such as a wire that attaches to walls and ceilings and doesn't lose signal strength.$(br2)Type $(6)@morered$() into $(emi) to see them all.

pages.title: Gates and Latches
pages.text: There are many other kinds of blocks that can control redstone. Most of them can be crafted by $(thing)stonecutting$() a $(item)Comparator$(), and can then be stonecut themselves, so you won't have to make lots of different devices to experiment.
A $(item)Pulse Timer$() can provide redstone pulses at arbitrary intervals, such as dropping items into a $(l:craftsmanship/blast_furnace)Blast Furnace$().
The $(item)Sequenced Pulse Generator$() can be configured to send a combination of redstone signals at varying time intervals.
Need to provide a constant signal strength? The $(item)Analog Lever$() is perfect for just that.
A $(item)Threshold Switch$() outputs a redstone signal based on how full a container is. It works with both items and fluids.
The $(item)Smart Observer$() is a more advanced version of a regular $(item)Observer$(). It can be filtered and can also detect changes in fluid levels.
The $(item)Redstone Link$() can transfer redstone signals wirelessly.

pages.title: Machine Covers
pages.text: $(thing)GregTech Covers$() can be placed directly onto your machines, and a lot of them will interact with redstone in some way. For example, the $(item)Machine Controller Cover$() lets you turn a machine off when it has a redstone signal.
